title: Renal Comprehensive Set 1: Urea, Calcium, Phosphate, Magnesium (Short Answer)

questions.prompt: What percentage of filtered urea is typically reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule, and what is the transport mechanism?
How does antidiuretic hormone (ADH) specifically increase urea reabsorption in the inner medullary collecting ducts?
questions.modelAnswer: It up-regulates the urea transporter UT1 (facilitated diffusion) in the inner medullary collecting duct.

questions.prompt: Explain the relationship between urine flow rate and urea excretion.
questions.modelAnswer: Urea excretion is directly proportional to urine flow rate; at high flow rates, less time is available for reabsorption, leading to increased excretion.

questions.prompt: Which segment of the nephron is responsible for approximately 85% of phosphate reabsorption?
By what intracellular signaling pathway does parathyroid hormone  inhibit phosphate reabsorption in the proximal tubule?
questions.modelAnswer: PTH activates adenylyl cyclase, generating cAMP, which inhibits the Na^+ -phosphate cotransporter in the luminal membrane.

questions.prompt: What is "urinary cAMP" (or nephrogenous cAMP), and what hormonal action does it represent?
questions.modelAnswer: It is cAMP produced in proximal tubule cells in response to PTH and secreted into the lumen; it serves as a marker for PTH action.

questions.prompt: Why is only 60% of total plasma calcium (Ca^(2+) ) filterable across the glomerular capillaries?
questions.modelAnswer: Because 40% of plasma Ca^(2+)  is bound to plasma proteins (primarily albumin) which cannot cross the filtration barrier.

questions.prompt: In which two nephron segments is Ca^(2+)reabsorption primarily passive and tightly coupled to Na^+  reabsorption?
questions.modelAnswer: The proximal tubule and the thick ascending limb.

questions.prompt: What is the electrochemical driving force for the paracellular reabsorption of Ca^(2+)and Mg2+  in the thick ascending limb?
questions.modelAnswer: The lumen-positive potential difference generated by the Na^+-K^+-2Cl^-cotransporter and K^+  back-leak.

questions.prompt: Why do loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide) cause an increase in urinary Ca^(2+)  excretion?
questions.modelAnswer: They inhibit Na^+-K^+-2Cl^-cotransport, which abolishes the lumen-positive potential that normally drives paracellular Ca^(2+)  reabsorption.

questions.prompt: How does the regulatory action of PTH on Ca^(2+)reabsorption in the distal tubule differ from its action on Na^+  reabsorption?
questions.modelAnswer: In the distal tubule, Ca^(2+)reabsorption is active and is not coupled to Na^+reabsorption; PTH increases Ca^(2+)  reabsorption here.

questions.prompt: Contrast the effect of thiazide diuretics on Na^+excretion versus Ca^(2+)  excretion.
questions.modelAnswer: Thiazides increase Na^+excretion (by inhibiting Na^+-Cl^-cotransport) but decrease Ca^(2+)excretion (by increasing Ca^(2+)  reabsorption).

questions.prompt: Unlike Na^+and Ca^(2+), which nephron segment is the major site (60%) of magnesium (Mg2+ ) reabsorption?
questions.modelAnswer: The thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle.

questions.prompt: Why does hypercalcemia lead to increased urinary excretion of Mg2+ ?
questions.modelAnswer: Ca^(2+)and Mg2+compete for reabsorption in the thick ascending limb; high Ca^(2+)levels inhibit Mg2+  reabsorption.

questions.prompt: Define "urea recycling" and state which hormone is required to augment this process.
questions.modelAnswer: Urea recycling is the movement of urea from the inner medullary collecting ducts into the medullary interstitial fluid and then into the thin descending limb; it is augmented by ADH.
